questions.q: What does SQL Server do when a parameterized query first compiles, that leads to parameter sniffing problems?
options: It builds a plan optimized specifically for the parameter value seen at that first execution
It ignores parameter values entirely and always builds a generic plan
It compiles a separate physical copy of the table for every parameter value
It disables the plan cache for that query permanently
questions.explain: SQL Server sniffs the actual parameter value at first compile and estimates row counts for that specific value using the statistics histogram.

questions.q: What kind of column is most likely to trigger a real parameter sniffing problem?
options: A skewed column where different values represent very different proportions of rows, like an order status
A column with a uniform distribution of unique values, like an identity primary key
Any column that is NOT NULL
Only computed columns
questions.explain: Skew (e.g. 2% Cancelled vs. 90% Shipped) means the optimal plan genuinely differs between values, so a plan sniffed for one value performs badly for another.

questions.q: What symptom in sys.dm_exec_query_stats specifically points at parameter sniffing rather than generic slowness?
options: A large gap between min_elapsed_time and max_elapsed_time for the same cached plan
A high total_logical_reads value alone
A plan_handle that is NULL
An execution_count of exactly one
questions.explain: The same cached plan running fast for some executions and slow for others (a big min/max elapsed time gap) is the signature of a plan mismatched to certain parameter values.

questions.q: What does adding OPTION (RECOMPILE) to a query do?
options: Forces a fresh plan, freshly sniffed for that call's actual parameter value, on every execution
Permanently disables parameter sniffing for the entire instance
Clears the entire plan cache for all queries
Converts the query into a Query Store-tracked query automatically
questions.explain: OPTION (RECOMPILE) trades a small per-execution compile cost for a plan that's always optimal for that call's specific parameter value.

questions.q: What does Parameter Sensitive Plan (PSP) optimization do, and when was it introduced?
options: It caches multiple plans for the same query and picks between them by parameter value; introduced in SQL Server 2022
It removes the need for statistics entirely; introduced in SQL Server 2016
It forces every query to always recompile; introduced in SQL Server 2012
It only applies to ad hoc queries, never stored procedures, since SQL Server 2005
questions.explain: PSP optimization, new in SQL Server 2022 and Azure SQL, lets the optimizer maintain multiple cached plans per query and choose based on the incoming parameter value.
